questions.stem: On hot days, red kangaroos lick their forearms, and the evaporating saliva cools the blood flowing just under the skin. What type of adaptation is the licking?
options: Vestigial
Behavioural
Structural
Physiological
questions.explanation: Licking is something the kangaroo does, so it is a behavioural adaptation. The network of blood vessels close to the skin of the forearm would be a structural adaptation, which is why the two are easy to mix up. A physiological adaptation is a process inside the body, such as producing very concentrated urine.

questions.stem: Spinifex grasses in central Australia have tightly rolled, needle-like leaves. How does this help them survive?
options: It shrinks the leaf surface exposed to hot, dry wind, cutting water loss
It increases the leaf area available to catch more of the strong sunlight
It lets each leaf store a large volume of water inside the rolled tube
It makes the leaves heavy enough that the wind cannot uproot the plant
questions.explanation: Rolling the leaf reduces the surface exposed to dry air and keeps the stomata on the inner side, so less water evaporates. Rolling does the opposite of increasing leaf area, and spinifex leaves are tough and dry rather than water-storing like a succulent. This is a structural adaptation to an arid habitat.

questions.stem: Weeks after a bushfire, a blackened eucalypt grows fresh leafy shoots straight out of its trunk and branches. Which feature makes this possible?
options: Seeds released from its woody fruit after the fire
Roots that send new shoots up through the burnt trunk
Epicormic buds protected beneath its thick bark
A lignotuber swollen at the base below the ground
questions.explanation: Epicormic buds lie dormant under the bark, which insulates them from the heat, and they sprout once the canopy has been burnt off. A lignotuber is also a fire adaptation, but it sends up shoots from the base at ground level, not along the trunk. Seeds released after a fire grow into new seedlings on the ground rather than shoots on the old tree.

questions.stem: Many banksias keep their seeds sealed inside woody follicles for years, and the follicles open only after a fire. Why is this an advantage?
options: The sealed follicles stop the parent plant from catching fire
The seeds fall onto ash-rich ground cleared of competing plants
The heat of the fire is needed to fertilise the ovules inside
The seeds germinate inside the follicle and drop as seedlings
questions.explanation: A fire removes the plants that would shade and compete with seedlings and leaves nutrients in the ash, so releasing seed then gives the seedlings their best chance. Fertilisation happened long before, when the flowers were pollinated, so the fire plays no part in it. Holding seed until a fire is a structural adaptation to Australia’s fire-prone bush.

questions.stem: During a drought, the water-holding frog of central Australia burrows underground, wraps itself in a cocoon of shed skin and stays inactive for months. What is this called?
options: Aestivation
Hibernation
Metamorphosis
Migration
questions.explanation: Aestivation is a dormant state that lets an animal survive hot, dry conditions with very little water or food. Hibernation is a similar dormancy but is a response to cold winter conditions, which is why it is the tempting answer. The frog emerges when heavy rain fills the claypans again.

questions.stem: Which of these features of the spinifex hopping mouse is a physiological adaptation?
options: Having long hind legs for hopping
Coming out to feed only at night
Producing very concentrated urine
Sheltering in a deep burrow by day
questions.explanation: A physiological adaptation is a body process, and the hopping mouse’s kidneys reabsorb so much water that it can survive without drinking. Sheltering in a burrow and being active only at night are behavioural adaptations, because they are things the animal does. Long hind legs are a body part, so they are structural.

questions.stem: What is an ectotherm?
options: An animal whose body temperature is always lower than its surroundings
An animal that makes most of its body heat from its own metabolism
An animal that can only survive in places colder than about 20 °C
An animal that gets most of its body heat from its surroundings
questions.explanation: Ectotherms such as lizards, snakes and frogs rely on the environment, for example sunlight or warm rocks, to heat their bodies. The old term ‘cold-blooded’ is misleading: a lizard basking in the sun can be warmer than the air around it. Making heat by metabolism is what endotherms such as mammals and birds do.

questions.stem: A bearded dragon lies on a sunny rock early in the morning before it goes hunting. Why?
options: To raise its body temperature so its muscles and enzymes work well
To absorb energy from sunlight that replaces the need to eat food
To dry its scales so that it loses less water during the hot day
To cool its body down after a long night of hunting in the dark
questions.explanation: As an ectotherm, the dragon’s body is cold after the night, and its muscles and enzymes work slowly until it warms up, so basking prepares it to move fast and catch prey. Sunlight provides heat, not the chemical energy found in food, so it still has to eat. Basking is a behavioural adaptation for controlling body temperature.

questions.stem: A 50 g mouse and a 50 g skink live in the same paddock. Which one needs to eat much more food each day, and why?
options: Both need the same, because their masses are the same
The skink, because its cold muscles waste more energy
The mouse, because it burns food to keep its body warm
The skink, because it must find heat as well as food
questions.explanation: An endotherm such as the mouse uses a large share of the energy in its food to keep its body temperature steady, so it needs several times more food than an ectotherm of the same mass. The skink gets its heat from the environment for free, which is why reptiles can go a long time between meals. Equal mass does not mean equal energy needs when one animal is making its own heat.

questions.stem: Why does a tiny honey possum lose body heat much faster, for its size, than a large kangaroo?
options: Its cells produce less heat than a kangaroo’s cells do
Its normal body temperature is much lower than a kangaroo’s
It has a larger surface area compared with its volume
It has a smaller surface area compared with its volume
questions.explanation: Heat is made throughout the body’s volume but lost through its surface, and small animals have far more surface area for each unit of volume. That is why small mammals lose heat quickly and must eat often to keep warm. Saying the honey possum has a smaller surface area to volume ratio reverses the relationship.

questions.stem: Two cube-shaped models of animals have sides of 1 cm and 3 cm. What are their surface area to volume ratios, and which model would lose heat faster for its size?
options: 6 : 1 and 3 : 1; the 1 cm cube loses heat faster
1 : 6 and 1 : 2; the 3 cm cube loses heat faster
6 : 1 and 2 : 1; the 1 cm cube loses heat faster
6 : 1 and 2 : 1; the 3 cm cube loses heat faster
questions.explanation: The 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 × 1 × 1 = 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, giving 6 : 1. The 3 cm cube has a surface area of 6 × 3 × 3 = 54 cm² and a volume of 27 cm³, giving 54 : 27 = 2 : 1. The larger ratio means more surface for heat to escape from each unit of volume, so the small cube loses heat faster.

questions.stem: On cold nights when food is scarce, some small marsupials such as the fat-tailed dunnart go into torpor. What happens, and how does it help?
options: Metabolism speeds up to burn stored fat as quickly as possible
The dunnart moves to a warmer district for the rest of the season
Body temperature and metabolism drop, saving energy until morning
Body temperature rises so the dunnart can stay active in the cold
questions.explanation: In torpor an endotherm lets its body temperature and metabolic rate fall for a few hours, which greatly reduces the food energy it would otherwise burn keeping warm. Hibernation is a longer version of the same strategy, lasting weeks or months. Raising body temperature would cost more energy, which is exactly what a small animal short of food cannot afford.

questions.stem: Humans sweat and dogs pant on hot days. What do both of these cooling methods rely on?
options: Reducing blood flow to the skin so heat stays inside
Slowing metabolism so that the body makes less heat
Evaporating water carrying heat away from the body
Releasing fluid that is colder than the surrounding air
questions.explanation: When water evaporates from the skin, or from the moist tongue and airways of a panting dog, it takes heat energy from the body with it. Sweat leaves the body at body temperature, so it does not cool by being cold. On hot days blood flow to the skin increases, not decreases, so that more heat can be lost.

questions.stem: A seedling on a windowsill grows so that it bends towards the window. What is this response called?
options: Negative phototropism
Positive gravitropism
Positive thigmotropism
Positive phototropism
questions.explanation: A tropism is a growth response towards or away from a stimulus; ‘photo’ means light, and ‘positive’ means growing towards it. Negative phototropism would mean bending away from the light. Gravitropism is a response to gravity and thigmotropism a response to touch.

questions.stem: A pot plant is laid on its side in a dark cupboard. After a few days the shoot has curved upwards and the root has curved downwards. Which description is correct?
options: The shoot and the root are both showing positive thigmotropism
The shoot is negatively gravitropic and the root is positively gravitropic
The shoot is positively gravitropic and the root is negatively gravitropic
The shoot is positively phototropic and the root is negatively phototropic
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls downwards, so the root growing down is growing towards the stimulus (positive) and the shoot growing up is growing away from it (negative). Swapping positive and negative is the common slip. Light cannot explain the result because the cupboard is dark.

questions.stem: When light shines on a shoot from one side, the plant hormone auxin moves to the shaded side of the tip. Why does the shoot then bend towards the light?
options: Cells on the shaded side lengthen more, pushing the tip towards the light
Cells on the lit side grow faster, pulling the tip over towards the light
Auxin is destroyed on the shaded side, so cells there stop growing at all
Light dissolves cell walls on the lit side, so that side of the shoot shrinks
questions.explanation: Auxin makes shoot cells elongate, so when it builds up on the shaded side those cells grow longer than the cells facing the light and the shoot curves towards the light. It is a common mistake to think the lit side does the work, but growth there is slower. The bend is caused by uneven growth, not by any side shrinking.

questions.stem: The tendrils of a pea plant coil around a garden stake as they grow. What is this response called?
options: Hydrotropism, a growth response to water
Phototropism, a growth response to light
Gravitropism, a growth response to gravity
Thigmotropism, a growth response to touch
questions.explanation: Where a tendril touches the stake, the cells on the far side grow faster, so it curls around the support and the plant can climb towards light. Touch is the stimulus here, which is what ‘thigmo’ refers to. The stake gives no water, light or change in gravity to respond to.

questions.stem: Tree roots often grow towards, and into, leaking underground water pipes. Which response best explains this?
options: Positive hydrotropism
Negative hydrotropism
Positive phototropism
Negative gravitropism
questions.explanation: Roots grow towards moisture, a positive response to water called hydrotropism, so the damp soil around a leak attracts them. Negative hydrotropism would mean growing away from water. Roots underground receive no light, and negative gravitropism would make them grow upwards.

questions.stem: The leaflets of the sensitive plant, Mimosa pudica, fold up within seconds when touched, whichever direction the touch comes from. Why is this a nastic movement rather than a tropism?
options: It is caused by slow growth rather than by water moving in cells
It happens only in response to light, never in response to touch
It is a permanent change that the plant can never reverse again
Its direction does not depend on the direction of the stimulus
questions.explanation: A tropism is directional growth towards or away from a stimulus, while a nastic movement happens the same way whatever direction the stimulus comes from. Mimosa folds quickly because cells at the base of each leaflet lose water and go limp, which is a change in turgor, not growth. The snapping trap of a Venus flytrap is another nastic movement.

questions.stem: Some trees shed many of their leaves during a long drought. How does this help them survive?
options: Without leaves, the tree takes in water through its bark
Without leaves, the tree can absorb more carbon dioxide
With fewer leaves, less water is lost by transpiration
With fewer leaves, the rate of photosynthesis increases
questions.explanation: Most water is lost through the stomata in leaves, so dropping leaves, like closing stomata, saves water when the soil is dry. The cost is that the tree makes less food by photosynthesis until it grows new leaves. Bark does not absorb water, and carbon dioxide enters through the leaves, so losing them reduces its uptake.

questions.stem: In biology, what is a stimulus?
options: A muscle or gland that carries out a reaction
A change in or around an organism that it can detect
The reaction an organism makes to a change around it
A specialised cell that detects changes in the body
questions.explanation: A stimulus is the change itself, such as light getting brighter or the body warming up. The reaction it causes is the response. Cells that detect stimuli are receptors, and the muscles or glands that react are effectors.

questions.stem: A person walks out of a dark cinema into bright sunlight and their pupils narrow. What is the stimulus?
options: The light-sensitive cells at the back of the eye
The increase in light reaching the eyes
The narrowing of the pupils in each eye
The muscles of the iris that change shape
questions.explanation: The stimulus is the change that is detected: the light getting brighter. The narrowing of the pupils is the response, the iris muscles are the effectors that produce it, and the light-sensitive cells are the receptors that detect the change.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the correct order of events when an animal responds to a stimulus?
options: Receptor, stimulus, response, effector
Response, receptor, effector, stimulus
Stimulus, receptor, effector, response
Stimulus, effector, receptor, response
questions.explanation: First something changes (the stimulus) and receptors detect it. The message is passed on, usually by nerves, to effectors such as muscles or glands, which carry out the response. A receptor has to detect a change before any effector can act on it.

questions.stem: In an animal, which part carries out the response to a stimulus?
options: A sense organ, such as the eye or the ear
An effector, which is a muscle or a gland
A receptor, which is a sense cell in an organ
A nerve, which carries the message along it
questions.explanation: Effectors are the muscles that move and the glands that release substances, so they produce the response. Receptors, often grouped in sense organs such as the eyes and ears, only detect the stimulus, and nerves carry the message between the two.

questions.stem: Which of these is an internal stimulus?
options: Bright light shining into the animal's eyes
The smell of a predator carried on the wind
A rise in the temperature of the blood
A sudden loud noise close to the animal
questions.explanation: An internal stimulus is a change inside the body, such as the blood warming up or the body running short of water. Noise, light and smells all come from the surroundings, so they are external stimuli.

questions.stem: On a hot day, receptors detect that a person's blood has warmed, and sweat glands release sweat onto the skin. In this response, what are the sweat glands?
options: Effectors
Receptors
Stimuli
Sense organs
questions.explanation: Glands, like muscles, are effectors: they carry out the response. The receptors are the cells that detected the warmer blood, and the stimulus is the rise in temperature itself. Sweating keeps body temperature steady, which is an example of homeostasis.

questions.stem: What is homeostasis?
options: Inheriting a feature that helps an organism survive in its habitat
Growing towards or away from a stimulus such as light or gravity
Keeping conditions inside the body steady when conditions outside change
Letting body temperature rise and fall to match the surroundings
questions.explanation: Homeostasis means keeping the internal environment, such as body temperature and water level, within a narrow range. Sweating, shivering and panting are all homeostatic responses. Matching body temperature to the surroundings is what ectotherms tend to do, and growing towards a stimulus is a tropism.

questions.stem: On a hot afternoon, a red kangaroo licks its forearms. Which pairing correctly identifies the stimulus and the response?
options: Stimulus: licking its forearms; response: its body temperature rising
Stimulus: the saliva evaporating; response: its blood cooling down
Stimulus: the skin of its forearms; response: saliva on its arms
Stimulus: its body temperature rising; response: licking its forearms
questions.explanation: The kangaroo detects that it is getting too hot, so the rise in body temperature is the stimulus, and licking is the response. The evaporating saliva and cooling blood are the result of the response, not the stimulus. Skin is a body part, not a change, so it cannot be a stimulus.

questions.stem: Why do most plant responses to a stimulus take hours or days, when many animal responses take less than a second?
options: Plants can respond only at night, when they are no longer photosynthesising
Plants usually respond by growing, controlled by hormones, not by nerves and muscles
Plants cannot detect a stimulus until it has gone on for at least a whole day
Plants respond only to changes inside their bodies, never to their surroundings
questions.explanation: Plants have no nerves or muscles. Most of their responses, such as a shoot bending towards light, happen when hormones like auxin change how fast cells grow, and growth is slow. Plants do detect outside stimuli such as light, gravity and touch, and they respond at any time of day.
